notes:
I could only do a small part of what you asked. My research tools hit their usage limit early, so I read just two sources: the Enduring Word page, which cut off partway through its notes on v. 1, and summaries of John Gill's Exposition from biblehub and studylight. I didn't get to read Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary, Precept Austin, Calvin, Matthew Henry, NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, or any Catholic, Orthodox or tradition-specific pages. As a result, Parts 2 and 3 are mostly empty, and the notes have no entries for vv. 13–14, 17, 22, 24–25 and 28–31.

**Part 1 – Traditional reading**

**Before v. 1 (how to read the chapter)**
- Guzik says we should take the Bible "literally" in the sense of reading each passage according to its kind of writing (history, poetry, prophecy). He says Genesis 1 has poetic features but records real history, not myth. He points to Psalm 136, which places creation in the same sequence as Israel's history, and says Jesus quoted Genesis as history. (The page cut off at that point.) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-1/

**v. 1**
- God is the subject of the Bible's first sentence. Guzik quotes Kidner's observation that "God" appears about 35 times in the chapter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-1/
- *Bara* ("created") means God made the world without using any existing material. It does not mean God made it out of Himself, so God is distinct from creation. Guzik contrasts this with Eastern and pantheistic ideas. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-1/
- Gill also says *bara* means bringing something new out of nothing, and notes the word is used only of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-1.html
- Guzik says the verse rules out the idea that the world came about by chance, since chance only describes a probability and causes nothing. He argues from design, citing Hugh Ross on the universe's "just-right" settings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-1/
- Gill says the verse shows the world is not eternal, against Aristotle, and was not formed by atoms moving at random. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/1.htm
- Gill's view of "heaven": some take it to mean the highest heaven where God and the angels dwell, and suggest the angels may have been created at this point. "Earth" here means the whole unformed mass of land and water before they were separated. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-1.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/1.htm
- Gill thinks the name *Elohim* comes from a root meaning "to worship." On that reading, Moses is teaching that the Creator alone should be worshipped. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/1.htm

**v. 2**
- Gill says the earth was a fluid mixture of land and water, not yet shaped. The Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem call it a waste and desert, empty of people, animals and plants. He says pagan myths of the world hatching from an egg grew out of the Spirit's "brooding" here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/1.htm

**v. 3**
- Gill suggests the divine Person speaking may be the Word (Logos) of John 1. He links the verse to 2 Corinthians 4:6: in the "new creation" of grace, light also comes first. He admits it is hard to say what this first light was. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/1.htm

**v. 4**
- Gill thinks the first light may have worked to thin out the chaos and form the air while the Spirit stirred the waters. He says God separated light from darkness so that they never share the same place and time, citing Job 38:24. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-1.html

**v. 5**
- Gill explains day and night on day one as a 24-hour cycle. Either the body of light circled the earth, or the unformed earth rotated toward it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-1.html
- He reports William Whiston's idea that each creation day equalled a year, but presents it as Whiston's view, not his own. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/1.htm

**vv. 6–8**
- Gill describes the expanse as something spread out like a curtain or tent. The verses about God "stretching out the heavens" refer to it, and the sun, moon and stars are placed in it (v. 17). In his view the "waters above" are the clouds that give rain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/1.htm
- He mentions two other views without adopting them: a store of water above the highest heaven (from which the Flood came), and a "crystalline heaven." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/1.htm

**vv. 9–10**
- Gill says the waters flowed into a basin made for them, at God's "rebuke." The name "earth" now applies only to the dry land. He also discusses why "it was good" appears here and not at day two: the separating of the waters was only finished now. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/1.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-1.html

**vv. 11–12**
- Gill says the moist ground could produce plants, but full-grown plants already bearing seed and fruit required God's almighty power. They appeared at once and in abundance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/1.htm

**vv. 15–16**
- Gill stresses that God made the lights himself. He says this shows the foolishness of worshipping the sun and moon, which are only servants placed for people's benefit. The sun "rules" the day, not people, even though pagans worshipped it as Molech and Baal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-1.html
- Gill quotes an early writer, whom the excerpt doesn't name, who argued that plants came before the stars to show that stars cannot be the cause of life on earth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-1.html

**v. 18**
- Gill says the repetition stresses the lights' proper purpose: they deserve due respect, but no more than that. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-1.html

**v. 19**
- Gill takes the day as one turn of the earth. He reports proposed calendar dates, including Archbishop Ussher's October 26. He draws a typology: the sun appeared on day four, and Christ, the "sun of righteousness," came in the fourth millennium. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-1.html

**vv. 20–21, 23**
- Gill says the waters had been made fruitful by the Spirit (v. 2) and brought forth the first animal life. The simpler creatures that "creep" or move came first. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-1.html

**v. 26**
- Gill rejects two Jewish readings of "Let Us": that God was speaking to the earth, or to the angels. He says angels are not God's counsellors and had no part in creation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-1.html

**v. 27**
- Gill finds God's image in several things: the body's upright form (pointing ahead to the body the Son would take), the immortal soul, the powers of the mind, the original holiness and righteousness, and the rule over creation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-1.html

**Part 2 – Where Protestant traditions differ**
I found almost nothing, apart from one partial point on v. 1:
- Do the plural *Elohim* and its singular verb point to the Trinity? Guzik quotes the Lutheran Luther and the Methodist Adam Clarke, who both say yes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-1/
- Gill, a Baptist, is more cautious. He says many hold this view, but the Trinity should be established on other grounds. He still says all three Persons took part in creation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/1.htm
- Luther's and Clarke's views reach us only through Guzik's quotes, not their own writings. I couldn't check Reformed, Pentecostal, Anglican or other teachers on any verse.

**Part 3 – Other views**
I didn't reach any modern-scholarship, Catholic, Orthodox or popular-teaching sources, so there is nothing to report.

The next sources to read would be Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary (both on biblehub), Precept Austin, NET Bible notes, newadvent.org, and a source on the length of the creation days in vv. 5 and 31, which is likely the main debated point among Protestants.
